ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Discrete Video Tokenizers for Low-Resource Training
PROPOSAL: Train and evaluate discrete video tokenizers using variational autoencoder (VAE) and diffusion-based initialization strategies, compared to a random initialization baseline. We will use the " Valley " tokenizer initialization strategy from " More robust discrete density modeling " as a control.
CONTROLS: Random initialization, Valley tokenizer, and diffusion-based initialization
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Diffusion-based initialization and Valley initialization will show improved quality over random initialization, but at varying levels of computational efficiency.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Coarse-to-Fine Video Generation with Scaled-Down Token Vocabulary
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the success of coarse-to-fine generation in image synthesis, implement a multi-scale autoregressive video generation framework that uses a series of scaled-down token vocabularies to sample tokens in a coarse-to-fine manner. We will compare this approach to a single, full-size vocabulary approach using the CONTROLS of the discrete video tokenizers investigation from experiment 1.
CONTROLS: Combination of proposed tokenizer initialization strategies, full-size vocabulary, and single-scale autoregressive generation
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The coarse-to-fine approach will show improved inference speed without a significant drop in quality, especially for longer videos and high-resolution frames, but may require careful tuning of the scale factor and vocabulary sizes.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Temporally-Aware Attention Mechanisms for Efficient Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Implement a hybrid attention mechanism that combines self-attention, cross-attention, and long-short term memory (LSTM) modules to efficiently capture temporal context while reducing computational overhead. We will evaluate its performance on both short and long video sequences using the LSDvid dataset, comparing it to a control setup that uses only self-attention.
CONTROLS: Self-attention only, LSTM-based attention
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The temporally-aware attention mechanism will show improved performance on long video sequences, capturing the coherent motion of objects over time, while not significantly increasing inference latency for short sequences. However, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance performance and speed.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED: Coarse-to-Fine Video Generation with Adaptive Vocabulary and Sampling Schedules
PROPOSAL: Modify the multi-scale autoregressive video generation framework to dynamically adjust the vocabulary size and sampling schedule based on the input sequence and generated frames. This adaptation will be achieved using a learnable temperature schedule and vocabulary resizing mechanism. We will evaluate its performance on video UFO and Vimeo-90k datasets, comparing it to a control setup that uses a fixed vocabulary and sampling schedule.
CONTROLS: Fixed vocabulary and sampling schedule, combination of proposed tokenizer initialization strategies
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive vocabulary and sampling schedule will improve the model's ability to handle varying video resolutions and content complexity, achieving better visual quality and efficiency on a wider range of input sequences. However, it may require significant computational resources and hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Mixed-Precision Training for Efficient Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of mixed-precision training (MPT) to reduce the computational cost and memory requirements of the discrete autoregressive video generation model. We will compare the performance of the model when trained with MPT (using a combination of fp32, fp16, and INT8 precision) to the original fp32 training setup.
CONTROLS: fp32 training only
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The mixed-precision training approach will significantly reduce the training time and memory requirements of the model without compromising its performance on the test set. However, the optimal mixed-precision configuration may require careful tuning to balance accuracy and efficiency.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Tokenization Strategies on Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of different tokenization strategies, including learnable tokenizers, learned discrete distributions, and discrete autoencoders, on the video generation task. We will evaluate their impact on visual quality, inference speed, and training stability.
CONTROLS: Random discrete distribution, Valley tokenizer initialization
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learnable tokenizers and learned discrete distributions will outperform the random discrete distribution in terms of visual quality, while the discrete autoencoders will provide a good trade-off between quality and training stability. However, the optimal tokenization strategy may depend on the specific video generation task and dataset.

ACTION: REVISION 1
TITLE: REVISION: Investigating Discrete Video Tokenizers for Low-Resource Training
PROPOSAL: Modify the discrete video tokenizer initialization strategies to include a cross-modal pre-training step, where the tokenizer is pre-trained on a large-scale image-text dataset before being fine-tuned on the video data. This will allow the tokenizer to capture more generalizable and robust representations.
CONTROLS: Diffusion-based initialization, Valley tokenizer, random initialization (original settings)
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The cross-modal pre-training step will improve the tokenizer's ability to generalize to video data, especially in low-resource scenarios, and will result in higher-quality videos. However, it may require additional computational resources and hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Long-Term Video Generation through Hierarchical Planning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical planning mechanism that allows the model to reason about the long-term video generation process by breaking it down into smaller, manageable tasks. This will enable the model to generate videos of arbitrary length without significant degradation in quality.
CONTROLS: Baseline autoregressive model without planning mechanism
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hierarchical planning mechanism will significantly improve the model's ability to generate long videos, but may require careful tuning of the planning strategy and hyperparameters to balance quality and computational efficiency.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Interactive Video Generation through Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop an interactive video generation framework that uses reinforcement learning to generate videos responsive to user input. The model will be trained to maximize a reward function that evaluates the coherence and relevance of the generated video to the user's input.
CONTROLS: Baseline video generation model without reinforcement learning, a random policy
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The reinforcement learning approach will enable the model to generate interactive videos that respond to user input in a coherent and relevant manner, but may require careful tuning of the reward function and hyperparameters to balance exploration and exploitation.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: A Unified Framework for Text-to-Image, Text-to-Video, Image-to-Video, and Video Extrapolation
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework that integrates all the previous experiments and mechanisms to enable the generation of high-quality videos given text, images, or other video inputs. The framework will be evaluated on its ability to generalize across different input modalities and scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baseline models for each individual task
COST: N/A (this is a meta-experiment combining the previous results)
PREDICTION: The unified framework will demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on all individual tasks and exhibit good generalization across different input modalities and scenarios. However, the optimal architecture and hyperparameters may require careful tuning to achieve the best results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating přip properties of discrete video tokenizers
PROPOSAL: Analyze how the quality of discrete video tokenizers trained on static images affects video synthesis performance in autoregressive models. Compare the reconstruction quality and spatiotemporal perception of tokenizers pre-trained on images to those fine-tuned on video datasets only. Evaluate the trade-offs between tokenizer pre-training, fine-tuning, and performance for both short and long video generation.
CONTROLS: Training a diffused video model on different tokenizer options, ablation study on tokenizer composition and optimization techniques.
COST: 10 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Pre-training on images provides a good enough initialization for fine-tuning, high tokenizer quality requires significant fine-tuning data and computational power, and our model struggles with fusing background and foreground information in videos, often resulting in partially rendered frames.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Discrete Video Tokenizer with Temporal-aware Weight Sharing
PROPOSAL: Design a discrete video tokenizer that incorporates temporal-aware weight sharing to capture the dynamics of video sequences. Shares weights across tokens within the same frame and across time steps to encourage coherent motion and reduce the difficulty of fine-tuning tokenizers for video data. Evaluates the impact on tokenizer performance for different video durations and compare to baselines without weight sharing.
CONTROLS: Compare with previous tokenizers that lack temporal-aware weight sharing, examine the influence of the weight sharing strategy on the final output.
COST: 20 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Performance improvement by integrating the proposed temporal-aware weight sharing mechanism; when tokenizers are pre-trained on image data, the videos they generate have coherent motion, and the qualitative changes between frames are similar for less object movements in a scene.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Inference of Autoregressive Video Generators
PROPOSAL: Propose an efficient inference framework for our autoregressive video generator that allows for fast and stable generation of video sequences. This involves incorporating a novel look-ahead mechanism that enables the model to predict a series of frames at each step, rather than generating individual frames sequentially. Additionally, we explore techniques such as caching, pruning, and knowledge distillation to further reduce computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Compare with previous approaches to efficient inference in autoregressive models, evaluate the trade-off between model accuracy and inference speed, and study the impact of look-ahead and caching on video quality.
COST: 30 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Significant speedup in inference time without compromising video quality, look-ahead mechanism shows improved performance on long video sequences, and caching techniques offer moderate gains in terms of speed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robust Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Integrate adversarial training into our autoregressive video generator to improve its robustness against video processing algorithms and attacks. We propose a novel adversarial loss function that combines perceptual and structural losses to guide the generator towards more realistic and robust video outputs. Additionally, we investigate the use ofdifferent types of adversarial examples, such as video noise, jitters, and packet losses, to further challenge the generator.
CONTROLS: Compare with previous approaches to adversarial training in generative models, evaluate the impact of adversarial training on video quality and robustness, and study the effect of different adversarial examples on the generator's performance.
COST: 40 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Significant improvement in video quality and robustness against typical video processing algorithms, adversarial training leads to a moderate increase in training time and energy consumption, and experiments on edge cases reveal a limited impact of adversarial examples on the generator's performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interactive Video Generation: Conditioning on User Input
PROPOSAL: Extend our autoregressive video generator to support interactive video generation, where the model can condition on user input and generate custom video sequences. We propose a novel interactive setup, where the user can provide hints or keywords that influence the video generation process. The generator will then adapt to the user's input and produce a unique video sequence that aligns with their preferences.
CONTROLS: Compare with previous approaches to interactive video generation, evaluate the impact of user input on video quality and relevance, and study the effect of different interactive modalities (e.g., text, image, audio).
COST: 60 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Significant improvement in video relevance and user satisfaction, interactive video generation leads to a moderate increase in computational overhead, and experiments on different interactive modalities reveal a unique set of strengths and weaknesses for each approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation and Comparison of Video Generation Models
PROPOSAL: Perform a comprehensive evaluation and comparison of our autoregressive video generator with state-of-the-art video generation models. We will assess the quality, diversity, and robustness of the generated videos using a range of metrics, including video metrics (PSNR, SSIM), diversity metrics (Intra-class coherence, Variance), and robustness metrics (Adversarial examples, Perturbation tolerance). Additionally, we will conduct user studies to evaluate the generated videos in terms of aesthetic appeal and coherence.
CONTROLS: Compare with previous approaches to video generation, evaluate the generalization ability of the proposed models on different datasets and tasks, and study the impact of hyperparameters on the video generation process.
COST: 80 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our proposed autoregressive video generator achieves state-of-the-art results on video quality and diversity metrics, shows robustness against adversarial attacks, and performs well in user studies, although it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenizer for VAR Models
PROPOSAL: We will propose a novel video tokenizer that is pre-trained on a large-scale video dataset and finetuned on a specific application, while learning to normalize and draw from a common pool of latent vectors that capture both spatial and temporal information through each step of a refinement cascade. The tokenizer would be specifically designed to handle video input by integrating temporal self-attention, or incrementally building upon a proven tokenizer from the image domain.
CONTROLS: Compare against variants of established image tokenizers with and without our new video transformer component; ablate temporal self-attention versus incremental building blocks.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By reusing existing image tokenizer weights, we can significantly reduce training time and initially reach a good balance between visual quality and inference speed. However, particularly long videos might strain the initial image tokenizer's ability to capture temporal dynamics, necessitating the development of more specialized models, such as possible revisions of our proposed video tokenizer, with possibly disappointing impact on the visual quality.

TITLE: Initializing VAR Model Weights with Pre-Trained Image and Video Models
PROPOSAL: We propose initializing VAR model weights using pre-trained weights from state-of-the-art image and video models. Specifically, we will experiment with initializing the early stages of the VAR model with pre-trained weights from a diffusion model on static images, and the late stages with pre-trained weights from a diffusion model on videos. We will also investigate initializing with weights from fully pre-trained image or video GANs for our mid and full recovery tasks. This could assist in achieving high-quality video and image synthesis with greater efficiency, reduce overfitting and the challenges of constrained data of the appearance locality gaps of temporal gaps.
CONTROLS: Compare against random initialization and ablate the effect of initializing different stages of the VAR model with pre-trained weights from image and video models.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will demonstrate how pre-trained weights can alleviate the issues of high variance during the training of VAR models, potentially leading to significant speedups in convergence time, reduced overfitting, and increased visual quality. ACTION: REVISE 3 
REASON: Simplify the proposal and make it more specific.
TITLE: Initializing VAR Model Weights with Pre-Trained Image Models
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with initializing the first stages of the VAR model with pre-trained weights from state-of-the-art image models (e.g. DALL-E, CLIP), and evaluate the effect on video synthesis quality and training stability.
CONTROLS: Compare against random initialization and ablate the effect of initializing a specific number of stages with pre-trained weights from image models.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will demonstrate how pre-trained image model weights can aid in initializing the VAR model, potentially leading to improved video synthesis quality and reduced training instability. However, there might be limitations when adapting to video specifics, affecting the quality in later stages.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Token Vocabulary Size on VAR Model Performance
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with varying the token vocabulary size of the VAR model, and evaluate its impact on video synthesis quality, training stability, and inference speed. We will explore both small and large vocabulary sizes, as well as different sampling strategies for generating tokens.
CONTROLS: Compare against a fixed, medium-sized token vocabulary, and ablate the effect of different vocabulary sizes on video synthesis quality and training stability.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Increasing the token vocabulary size may allow the model to capture more detailed and nuanced visual features, leading to improved video synthesis quality, but it may also lead to increased inference time and computational costs. Reducing the vocabulary size may lead to faster inference and training times, but may compromise video synthesis quality.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Temporal Modeling using Hierarchical Motion Representations in VAR Models
PROPOSAL: We will incorporate hierarchical motion representations into the VAR model to improve its ability to capture temporal dynamics and motion patterns in videos. This will involve learning compact motion representations at multiple scales and using them to refine the video synthesis process.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline VAR model without hierarchical motion representations, and ablate the effect of different motion representation architectures on video synthesis quality.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hierarchical motion representations should allow the model to capture more nuanced and complex motion patterns, leading to improved video synthesis quality and more realistic motion in generated videos. However, this may also increase the computational cost and training time of the model.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Interactive Video Generation using Context-aware VAR Models
PROPOSAL: We will extend the VAR model to support interactive video generation by incorporating a context-aware mechanism that allows the model to respond to user feedback and adjust its output accordingly. This will involve training the model on a dataset of interactive videos and evaluating its ability to learn from user feedback and generate responsive video content.
CONTROLS: Compare against a non-interactive VAR model, and ablate the effect of different context-aware mechanisms on video synthesis quality and responsiveness to user feedback.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The context-aware VAR model should be able to learn from user feedback and generate responsive video content, leading to improved interactive video generation performance. However, this may also increase the computational cost and training time of the model, and require careful tuning of the context-aware mechanism to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluating Zero-Shot Video Synthesis using VAR Models
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the ability of the VAR model to perform zero-shot video synthesis, i.e., generating videos without any explicit guidance or conditioning on a specific visual concept or action. This will involve training the model on a large dataset of videos and evaluating its ability to generalize to unseen visual concepts and actions.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline VAR model trained with explicit guidance, and ablate the effect of different training strategies and architectures on zero-shot video synthesis performance.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The VAR model should be able to achieve impressive zero-shot video synthesis performance, especially when combined with the hierarchical motion representations and context-aware mechanisms explored in previous experiments. However, there may still be limitations in its ability to capture complex visual concepts and actions, requiring further exploration of advanced architectures and training strategies.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Large-Scale Evaluation of VAR Models on Real-World Video Data
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of the VAR model on a large-scale, real-world video dataset, encompassing diverse visual concepts, actions, and scenarios. This will involve training the model on a subset of the dataset and evaluating its performance on the remaining subset, as well as comparing it to state-of-the-art video synthesis models.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art models, ablate the effect of different training strategies and architectures on performance, and evaluate the model's performance on various metrics, such as video quality, realism, and diversity.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The VAR model should achieve competitive performance on real-world video data, especially when combined with the architectures and training strategies explored in previous experiments. However, there may still be limitations in its ability to generalize to diverse visual concepts and actions, requiring further exploration of advanced architectures and training strategies.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: System Design and Implementation of a High-Performance VAR Model Pipeline
PROPOSAL: We will design and implement a high-performance pipeline for the VAR model, including optimized data loading, model inference, and post-processing steps. This will involve developing a custom framework for scaling up the model to handle large batches of input data and producing high-quality video outputs at real-time.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline implementation, and ablate the effect of different optimizations and tweaks on performance and video quality.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The optimized pipeline should significantly improve the performance and efficiency of the VAR model, enabling real-time video synthesis and generation on large inputs. However, the complexity of the system design may lead to potential stability issues, requiring careful tuning and testing to ensure robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Decomposition of Video Generators
PROPOSAL: We propose decomposing the autoregressive video generator into a hierarchy of sub-modules, where each sub-module is responsible for modeling a specific aspect of the video (e.g., background, motions, foreground objects). This hierarchical decomposition allows us to model both spatial and temporal dependencies efficiently and reduce the computational cost. We will design each sub-module to be highly specialized and reconfigurable to accommodate various input formats (e.g., text, image, video) and generation tasks (e.g., text-to-video, image-to-video).
CONTROLS: We will compare our hierarchical decomposition approach against existing video generators and evaluate its performance using metrics such as Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Multi-Scale Structural Similarity (MS-SSIM).
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our hierarchical decomposition approach is expected to achieve a significant reduction in inference latency (~30% reduction) while maintaining comparable visual quality to state-of-the-art methods. However, it may struggle to capture complex motion and scene changes, leading toissetlications in its performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenizer via Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We propose using knowledge distillation to transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained discrete image tokenizer to a discrete video tokenizer, allowing for efficient multi-modal learning. Specifically, we will fine-tune the discrete image tokenizer on video-specific tasks, such as frame-level reconstruction, and use the distilled knowledge to guide the learning of the discrete video tokenizer. This approach is expected to reduce the training cost and improve the reconstruction quality of the discrete video tokenizer.
CONTROLS: We will compare our knowledge distillation approach against training discrete video tokenizers from scratch and against initializing discrete video tokenizers from pre-trained discrete image tokenizers without knowledge distillation.
COST: Estimated 50 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our knowledge distillation approach is expected to reduce the training cost by ~60% while achieving comparable reconstruction quality to training discrete video tokenizers from scratch. However, it may struggle to capture video-specific features and distributions, leading to reduced performance in certain video generation tasks.

ACTION: REVISETurn 1
TITLE: Hierarchical Decomposition of Video Generators
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL We propose integrating our previous hierarchical decomposition approach with the efficient discrete video tokenizer via knowledge distillation. Specifically, we will use the distilled knowledge from the discrete image tokenizer to guide the learning of the discrete video tokenizer in each sub-module of the hierarchical decomposition. This integrated approach is expected to achieve significant improvements in both inference latency and visual quality.
CONTROLS: We will compare our integrated approach against combining the standalone hierarchical decomposition approach and the standalone knowledge distillation approach.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our integrated approach is expected to achieve a ~45% reduction in inference latency and a ~15% improvement in visual quality compared to state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining the advantages of both individual approaches. However, it may still struggle to capture complex motion and scene changes, leading to additional challenges in its performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Long-Short Term Memory for Temporal Consistency
PROPOSAL: We propose incorporating a Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) mechanism into our hierarchical decomposition approach to maintain temporal consistency and capture both short-term and long-term dependencies in videos. The LSTM mechanism will be used to process the generated frames sequentially, updating the temporal context and adjusting the generation accordingly. This approach is expected to significantly improve the performance of our hierarchical decomposition approach in video extrapolation and long interactive video generation.
CONTROLS: We will compare our LSTM-based approach against using a simple recurrent unit (SRU) and a gated recurrent unit (GRU) for temporal processing.
COST: Estimated 80 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our LSTM-based approach is expected to achieve a significant improvement in temporal consistency (~20% improvement in PSNR) and video quality (~10% improvement in MS-SSIM) compared to the hierarchical decomposition approach without LSTM. However, it may lead to additional computational cost and training complexity, making it harder to achieve convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Aware Attention for Efficient Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose incorporating task-aware attention mechanisms into our hierarchical decomposition approach to adaptively focus on the most relevant information for each generation task. Specifically, we will design a task-specific attention module that learns to selectively attend to different aspects of the input data (e.g., text, image, video) and generate the corresponding video tokens. This approach is expected to improve the efficiency and accuracy of our hierarchical decomposition approach in various video generation tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our task-aware attention approach against using fixed attention mechanisms and against not using attention.
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our task-aware attention approach is expected to achieve a ~15% improvement in efficiency (reduced number of computations) and a ~5% improvement in video quality (PSNR) compared to the hierarchical decomposition approach without attention. However, it may lead to additional training complexity and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISETurn 3
TITLE: Long-Short Term Memory for Temporal Consistency
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL We propose integrating our LSTM mechanism with the task-aware attention module to adaptively focus on the most relevant information for temporal consistency. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Temporal Modeling for Image-to-Video, Text-to-Video, and Video Extrapolation
PROPOSAL: To unify our previous work on temporal modeling for pure discrete autoregressive video generation (proposal 1) and long-interactive video generation (proposal 4), we will develop a novel unified temporal modeling framework that can seamlessly integrate different temporal modeling strategies, data modalities, and generation tasks. Our framework will enable state-of-the-art performance on image-to-video, text-to-video, and video extrapolation tasks, while also being modular and easily extensible to new generation tasks and data modalities.
CONTROLS: Our controls will include a fixed-length transformer baseline and the state-of-the-art video diffusion model VQ-VAE-2 for each of the three generation tasks.
COST: Estimated 6,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our unified temporal modeling framework will achieve state-of-the-art performance on all three generation tasks, while also demonstrating improved efficiency, scalability, and flexibility compared to existing models.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Unified Temporal Modeling for Image-to-Video, Text-to-Video, and Video Extrapolation
PROPOSAL: We will revise our unified temporal modeling framework (proposal 5) to incorporate the insights and findings from our previous experiments, including the importance of discrete video tokenizers, multimodal fusion, and lightweight recurrent architectures. Our revised framework will be implemented as a single, end-to-end model that can handle all three generation tasks, and will be trained using a combination of supervised and self-supervised learning objectives. We will evaluate our revised framework on the OmniBSDS, UCF-101, and iViV datasets, and compare its performance to state-of-the-art models on each task.
CONTROLS: Our controls will include a fixed-length transformer baseline and the state-of-the-art video diffusion model VQ-VAE-2 for each of the three generation tasks, as well as our previously proposed models for each task.
COST: Estimated 8,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our revised unified temporal modeling framework will achieve state-of-the-art performance on all three generation tasks, while also demonstrating improved efficiency, scalability, and flexibility compared to existing models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generalizing Discrete Video Tokenizers through Multi-Resolution Pretraining
PROPOSAL: Investigate pretraining the discrete video tokenizer on a hierarchical dataset with images and low-resolution videos, and then fine-tune it on a high-resolution video dataset. This multi-resolution pretraining scheme aims to leverage the known strengths of image tokenizers while adapting to the complexities of video tokenization.
CONTROLS: Compare to a setup where the discrete video tokenizer is trained from scratch on the high-resolution video dataset, and to a setup where the weights are initialized from a discrete image tokenizer and fine-tuned on the high-resolution video dataset.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (2 days with 8 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Multi-resolution pretraining should significantly improve the quality of the discrete video tokenizer, reducing the training burden and allowing for faster convergence. However, it may come at the cost of increased computational requirements due to the pretraining step.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Temporal Modeling for Long Spatiotemporal Contexts
PROPOSAL: Design a novel attention mechanism that adaptively learns to attend to the relevant spatiotemporal context for each video token, rather than relying on fixed long-range dependencies. This is achieved by splitting the long-range context into smaller chunks and using a hierarchical attention mechanism to focus on the most relevant chunks.
CONTROLS: Compare to a standard self-attention mechanism, and to an ablation study where the attention mechanism is replaced with a fixed, sparse attention pattern.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (3 days with 8 GPUs)
PREDICTION: The proposed attention mechanism should significantly reduce the computational cost of processing long spatiotemporal contexts, while maintaining or even improving the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies and preserve temporal consistency.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Efficient Temporal Modeling for Long Spatiotemporal Contexts
REVISED PROPOSAL: Modify the hierarchical attention mechanism to incorporate additional contextual information, such as the similarity between tokens in the video sequence and in the input text. This is achieved by conditioning the attention weights on a learned encoding of the input text, allowing the model to better capture the semantic connections between video and text.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original hierarchical attention mechanism, and to an ablation study where the text conditioning is removed.
COST: No additional cost due to modification of previous proposal (still 150 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: The revised attention mechanism should improve the model's ability to capture complex semantic relationships between video and text, leading to better performance on tasks such as text-to-video generation and video extrapolation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bitwise Modeling for Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Adapt the bitwise modeling technique from Infinity (for image generation) to video generation by representing each video token as a sequence of bits, and using a learnable transform to map the input text and previous tokens to the bit sequence of the current token.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original autoregressive model without bitwise modeling, and to an ablation study where the learnable transform is replaced with a fixed, hand-designed transform.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (2.5 days with 8 GPUs)
PREDICTION: The bitwise modeling technique should improve the model's ability to generate high-quality video, particularly for long sequences, by capturing more detail and nuance in the video signal. However, it may also increase the computational cost due to the additional transformations required.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unifying Text-to-Image and Text-to-Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Use a shared embedding space for the text encoders in both text-to-image and text-to-video tasks, allowing the model to leverage shared knowledge and improve performance across both tasks. Additionally, use a multi-tasking loss function that combines losses from both tasks to encourage the model to develop a more general understanding of the input text.
CONTROLS: Compare to separate text encoders for each task, and to a baseline where only one task is used for training.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (1.7 days with 8 GPUs)
PREDICTION: The shared embedding space and multi-tasking loss should enable the model to generalize better across tasks and improve performance on both text-to-image and text-to-video generation. However, it may also increase the complexity of the model and require additional computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Guided Generation for Video Extrapolation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a guided loss function that encourages the model to generate new video frames that are consistent with the input text and the previously generated frames. This is achieved by computing a similarity score between the generated frames and a set of conditioned reference frames, and incorporating this score into the loss function.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline where the model is trained without the guided loss function, and to an ablation study where the conditioned reference frames are replaced with randomly sampled frames.
COST: 140 GPU-hours (3 days with 8 GPUs)
PREDICTION: The guided generation approach should improve the model's ability to generate high-quality new frames for video extrapolation, particularly in situations where the input text contains sufficient context for the model to understand what comes next. However, it may also increase the risk of mode collapse or overfitting if not balanced properly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pose-Guided Video Generation for Interactive Video Sequences
PROPOSAL: Introduce a pose-guided loss function that encourages the model to generate video frames that are consistent with the input text and the pose information of the subjects in the scene. This is achieved by computing a similarity score between the generated frames and a set of conditioned reference frames, and incorporating this score into the loss function.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline where the model is trained without the pose-guided loss function, and to an ablation study where the conditioned reference frames are replaced with randomly sampled frames.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (4 days with 8 GPUs)
PREDICTION: The pose-guided video generation approach should improve the model's ability to generate high-quality interactive video sequences that are consistent with the input text and the pose information of the subjects. However, it may also increase the complexity of the model and require additional computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Discrete Autoregressive Video Models to Distribution Shifts
PROPOSAL: Perform a thorough evaluation of the robustness of the proposed discrete autoregressive video model to distribution shifts, including variations in image resolution, pose, lighting, and action.
CONTROLS: Compare to a state-of-the-art diffusion-based video model that is known to be robust to distribution shifts.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (1.3 days with 8 GPUs)
PREDICTION: The discrete autoregressive video model should demonstrate competitive robustness to distribution shifts compared to the diffusion-based video model, due to its ability to capture temporal dependencies and generate high-quality video frames in a variety of scenarios. However, its performance may degrade in cases where the distribution shift is extreme or unrealistic.

TITLE: Long-Term Video Generation with Actor-Critic Methods
PROPOSAL: Employ actor-critic methods, such as Actor-Critic Models (ACMs) or Learning to Predict Gradual Changes (LG), to enable the discrete autoregressive video model to generate long-term video sequences that are coherent and temporally consistent.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline where the model is trained without actor-critic methods, and to an ablation study where the ACM/LG is replaced with a standard policy gradient method.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (4.5 days with 8 GPUs)
PREDICTION: The actor-critic approach should enable the discrete autoregressive video model to generate high-quality long-term video sequences that are temporally consistent and coherent. However, it may also increase the risk of overfitting or instability if not balanced properly.
